newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia shows off its low inflation credentials.
newsitem.headline: Australia shows off its low inflation credentials.

text.p: Australia's growing reputation as a low inflation economy was cemented on Wednesday with the release of tame inflation data, and the result was welcomed by both the government and economists.

Although the continued improvement in inflation has not guaranteed a fourth interest rate cut, it has given the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) the room to reduce rates if it needed to, economists said.
The central bank has lowered interest rates three times since July last year.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose by a mild 0.2 percent in the quarter to December 31, to be 1.5 percent higher over 1996.
It was the smallest quarterly rise since the last quarter of 1993 and the lowest annual rate since the first 1994 quarter.

The closely watched underlying rate, which excludes certain volatile factors, rose 0.4 percent in the quarter to be 2.1 percent higher over 1996. It was the lowest annual rate since the March 1995 quarter.
The underlying rate is the inflation measure the RBA focuses on when setting monetary policy.
"Australia is now decisively in a period of low inflation, Treasurer Peter Costello told reporters on Wednesday after the CPI data were released.
"We are one of the low inflation countries of the world."
Economists generally agreed with that assessment.

Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton saw the data as "confirming Australia's status as a bona fide member of the low inflation league," and said further improvement in inflation results is likely this year.

"Today's numbers continue the run of good outcomes which should be increasingly seen as a structural shift to low inflation rather than some temporary aberration," Commonwealth Bank senior economist Michael Blythe said.
Treasurer Costello said the fall in inflation was consistent with the RBA's inflation objectives, and would contribute to a lower interest rate environment.
Over the past few years, the central bank has aimed to keep the underlying inflation rate at an average between two and three percent.

Economists said they expect inflation to remain off their list of concerns through 1997, with the effects of the Australian dollar's rise through 1996 yet to be seen, and continued subdued growth in partial price indicators.

"There are no obvious threats to near term inflation," Citibank Australia economists said in a commentary, adding that annual underlying inflation could fall to under 1.8 percent in the June quarter, which would be the lowest level in the series' 25-year history.
Despite the positive outlook, economists said low inflation alone was not sufficient to justify a rate cut after next week's RBA board meeting.

The deciding factors would be developments in economic activity and wages growth, particularly the outcome of the Australian Council of Trade Unions' (ACTU) claims for pay rises for lower-paid workers, which begin at 8.75 percent.
The RBA warned last month that acceptance of the full claim "would imply a marked acceleration of wages growth."
In recent years, one of the central bank's main concerns has been the pace of wages growth. A significant acceleration would have an undesirable effect on inflation.
Societe Generale chief economist John Edwards said that while there was room for a rate cut, he was not expecting one as soon as next week.

"With three cuts behind it, the RBA is now likely to wait and see both the December quarter average weekly earnings numbers next week, and the Industrial Relations Commission (decision) on the ACTU's claim in February or March," he said.
